utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have the appearances, please. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, David Re and Ekkehard Withopf, with Kimberly Fleming as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo; Stephane Bourgon, attorney from Montreal; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for Mr. Kubura, may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Mr. Rodney Dixon, and legal assistant Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber would like to say good afternoon to all the people attending this afternoon's sitting. Before the witness is brought in, I should like to remind you of certain points with respect to procedure, procedure put in place. With respect to written motions, we were seized of this by the Defence, an application from the Defence, with respect to access of the archives of the ECMM. I should now like to call upon the Prosecution to let me know in writing what their position is until 9.00 Monday morning. Next Monday morning, 9.00, may we have that in writing please. Why? Because we have to make a ruling as soon as possible. And in view of the fact that we're going to have an interruption -- a break of three week's time, we should like to know the position of the Prosecution as of Monday, which will allow the Trial Chamber to make a ruling in the week that follows; that is to say, next week. So unless we receive this by 9.00 on Monday morning from the Prosecution, we shall take it that the Prosecution has no observations to make with respect to the motion filed by the Defence. Would the Prosecution like to say anything in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we just received the Defence motion. We will file a response. It will likely be a very brief response, by Monday at 9.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We were also informed that there was a motion from the Prosecution with respect to the list of witnesses and exhibits, and there will be a deadline, which is the 12th of January, for the Defence to let us have their observations with respect to that list. I'd like to remind them of that. So would they let us know in time. There was a third point -- or rather, two other pending issues. The Defence, with regard to the coming -- or rather, the Defence indicated in the past few days that it would like to inform us of a written motion with respect to testimony from other trials. So I'm waiting for that motion to be filed by the Defence. And once again, could they please do so in time and as soon as possible, in actual fact. With respect to the other issue, allowing the Prosecution to proceed to a cross-examination once a witness -- when the oral testimony of a witness differs from his written statement, the Prosecution has informed us in writing about that and I assume that Defence -- the Defence will be provided with that document. I have just received it, so I'm sure you will too. And once you have received it, I'll invite the Defence to inform me of their position quickly so that we can rule. So please do your best to respond as quickly as possible. I should like to remind you all that when there are motions concerning important problems, basic problems of law, written motions are better than oral applications. It is more precise and exact, which means that the response and answer will be more precise, rather than having an oral ruling. Of course, if we can find oral solutions to matters that are not as serious, then we invite oral applications, of course. But if you feel that they are questions which have to do with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and you feel that certain stipulations should be included into the Rules and are not, then we invite written motions. If the parties have nothing more to add at this point - unless the Defence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic would like to take the floor, or the Prosecution - they're on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Can I just correct something. The motion which the Prosecution filed today, fairly -- I think about an hour ago, is in fact a motion for reconsideration of your -- of the Trial Chamber's ruling of last Wednesday, or in the alternative, for certification for an interlocutory appeal. That is not, in fact, the motion in respect of cross-examination of adverse witnesses. The Prosecution is in the process of writing that motion. We clearly couldn't have done it overnight or this morning, because it requires some research and a bit more time. We will have that filed sometime early next week, I would anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are referring to an oral ruling given on Wednesday, are you? And could you explain what you mean? Because I have the document before me, but we haven't had time to study it. So what was the query?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no query. Your Honours seem to be addressing the parties -- asking the Defence to respond to a motion Your Honour thought we had filed in respect of my application last night at about ten to 7.00, which was in respect of cross-examination or putting a -- cross-examination of a party's own witness. Your Honours ruled on Wednesday, the 4th of December, in relation to allowing the Prosecution to show a witness a prior statement given to an OTP investigator for the purposes of refreshing memory. Today the Prosecution under Rule 73(B), if they wish to ask the Trial Chamber to certify it as fit for an interlocutory appeal has seven days to do so. There's some debate -- and it's not quite settled within the Tribunal whether the seven days is today or tomorrow. To be on the safe side, we filed it today, rather than filing -- asking Your Honours for a motion asking for additional time. The motion is in two parts. It's firstly asking Your Honours to reconsidering your ruling in the light of an Appeals Chamber decision in the case of Simic and some other Trial Chamber rulings: Martinovic, Milosevic, Blagojevic, which we have referred Your Honours to. It's based upon the fact there was no proper legal argument. It was an oral argument. It came up in the middle of the trial. We're asking Your Honours to reconsider it in the light of considered legal submissions. The Defence, of course, has the normal ten days, or if Your Honours order a shorter period, to respond. So that's that one. The other motion we will file in writing, as Your Honours -- as Your Honour, the Presiding Judge requested last night. It relates to my application at about ten to 7.00. As I mentioned earlier, we just could not do it and do it properly to the standard which would be acceptable here. We won't be able to do that, because we're in trial at the moment, until early next week. We can certainly provide the Defence with a courtesy copy of this motion which we filed today if the Defence requires it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will respect the deadline and will give its stipulations by the 12th of January with respect to the requests made by the Prosecution, in view of new witnesses and exhibits and evidence. And before the deadline of the 12th of January that the Appeals Chamber set -- that the Trial Chamber set, we shall give our opinions as to the expert report. As we've already said, we can do this five days after we have received the translation -- or rather, the document in the B/C/S language. We have not received a B/C/S version to date, so we should like to ask the Prosecution to keep their promise and provide us with a copy by the 12th of this month, as they said they would. We should also like to prevail upon the Prosecution to send in the document to us that you have just received so that the Defence can state its views regarding that document too. Before the Christmas break - that is to say, by the end of next week - we shall file our own motion for exemption of the statements of the accused given in other trials. We feel that this is a very important question because the Prosecution has already sent you the expert report which is based on those statements, although we previously said that evidence of this kind and exhibits of this kind should not present -- be presented before the Trial Chamber rules on our own motion. We shall do our best to respond before the deadline set to the other Prosecution motions or any other Prosecution motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to raise a last point now: The Prosecution has informed us -- or rather, has disclosed a document to us which was the subject of the examination of the witness, and the number has -- there's a provisional number, which is P11 ID. It was marked for identification. The witness told us that he had no knowledge of that document, so I should now like to ask the Prosecution, which has produced this document, to tell us under what circumstances it came by the document and, if they would like to tender it into evidence and to present it, we should like to know where the document comes from, how they got it, and of course the -- they can present the document through another witness, because we just can't have documents turning up out of the blue in this way, especially if the witness says that he does not recognise it and has never seen it. So I should like to ask the Prosecution to explain how they came by this document, and of course if we don't admit it, you won't be able to use it. So could you please explain to us what the provenance of the document is. The Defence is well aware of this document. They've seen it. They know what it is. But they don't know the contents of it. It is number P11 ID; that is the number the document has. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we understand you're talking about the instructions to the Muslim fighters. The Prosecution got this document from different sources. One of the sources has been a search in October 2000 in the library of the 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica. The 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica is a successor unit of the 7th Muslim Brigade. The Prosecution got this document from additional sources as well, and the one the Prosecution has marked for identification is the one which has been tendered into evidence by the Defence in the Kordic case. For the time being, we wish to have this document only be marked for identification. The Prosecution will tender this document into evidence via a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the Defence like to say anything with respect to document P11? As we've just heard from the Prosecution today, that the document was discovered in the ancient headquarters of the 7th Brigade and that it can produce the document through a different witness. And they have asked us for -- that it be marked for identification. The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see a document in your hands -- or rather, the outside covers of the document, not the whole document. So I want to know what is being tendered, the whole document or just the cover. And the Prosecution themselves said that they found the document in the library when it was searched in 2000-and-I-don't-know-what year. We're dealing with events that took place in 1993. So that is not the right grounds for that, foundations. The document was not recognised by the witness, so I don't think we even have the necessary conditions to mark it for identification. Of course, if the Prosecution has a way of producing the document through another witness later on in the trial, I'm sure they'll do so, because they know what their job is and I'm sure they'll do everything according to the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an identical position to the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic; nothing to add there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a moment ago Your Honour I think said -- the transcript has just gone. The witness said something to the effect of he hadn't seen it before. I'm just reading from the transcript. I asked -- this is at page 42 of the running -- the running transcript. I asked the witness: "Q. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what the document on the left-hand side of the screen is." His answer was: "A. This document contained instructions that concerned the religion of soldiers who perhaps were not familiar with certain religious matters." My next question was: "Q. Who received this document?" The answer was: "A. Each and every soldier had access to this document. "Q. Did you receive a copy of this document yourself? "A. I consulted some of the literature that was available, but I do not remember whether I had a look at this copy. I don't remember whether I read it." I then asked him where it was kept and what he meant by "they had access to it," and he said: "A. You will just tort your hodza and see if -- the hodza would make an effort to provide you with the literature required." Now, at that point I intended to tender it. Perhaps I tried to tender it a little bit too prematurely, because it was fairly apparent from the exchange between the witness and me that he was familiar with the document by his answer "each and every document -- soldier had access to the document." The witness has in fact identified that type of document. It would appear that he was referring to -- he wasn't sure whether it was this exact copy, this precise copy, as opposed to familiarity with the document of this source. Now, that, in the Prosecution's submission, lays the foundation for it to be tendered at a later point, which, as Mr. Withopf told you a moment ago, we will attempt to do through another witness. The reason -- the Defence seems to be slightly concerned that Your Honours have a copy of it. It was marked for identification. The registry asked us to provide the required seven copies, so we in fact provided the required seven copies. Practices differ; in some Trial Chambers or jurisdictions the Bench doesn't see a document until it is actually tendered, unless there's some argument about its admissibility. And of course, as professional Judges, in the Prosecution's submission, it makes no difference. So that's why Your Honours have the document. We were attempting to speed things up by perhaps shortcutting, because I anticipated the witness was just going to identify it. And we showed it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to him on the screen in Sanction also in an attempt to speed proceedings up. That's why Your Honours have got several -- that's why it was shown to him on the screen and Your Honours now have a copy of it. But as Mr. Withopf says, we intend to fully tender it at a later point, so I would just ask it to be -- remain marked for identification at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned colleague quoted just part of the witness's answer, because the witness was just looking at the first page that you yourself have just shown us. And later on, during the examination, he was very uncertain as to which document it was. But not to make a problem out of this. We don't have anything against having it marked for identification and have this first page included. Of course, the Prosecution will have to prove whether the document was accessible to the members of the BH army, and if so, in what way, in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. While I have it in mind, if -- and as far as I remember, in the first part of his examination the witness gave certain indications to the document. With respect to the examination, he went back to his assertions. And when I asked him, his answer was that he had never actually seen the document. So if we quote the beginning of a testimony, we ought to quote the entirety as well. So it has been marked for identification as P11 ID. Of course, the Prosecution will be able to reintroduce the document in due course through other witnesses. Having said that, let us now start the cross-examination of the witness in hand. And I'd like to ask -- unless the Prosecution, of course, has anything to add. I should like to remind you that we -- the sitting today will last until 7.00 p.m. The witness has already been here several days. But having said that, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution is, of course, entirely mindful of time constraints. Yesterday, at the close of proceedings I realised that I had neglected to ask the witness several questions after the alleged death of -- sorry -- after the death of Zvonko Rajic relating to events in Dusina. I left it there and went on to another one because of what was happening. I just ask if I could perhaps be allowed to complete the examination-in-chief in relation to that aspect of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, maybe ten minutes, 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the Defence anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence needs an hour -- the Prosecution required an hour and a half for this witness, and they've been questioning him for a couple of days. At the end of the examination-in-chief the Prosecution said they had concluded the examination-in-chief, and I don't think that additional questions can be asked in this manner. If there is the opportunity to do so during the cross-examination, of course the Prosecution is at liberty to put questions then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday the Prosecution did tell us that they had finished with their examination, but they thought they would have leave to ask other questions in the course of the cross-examination with regard to an adverse witness. But as you know, the Trial Chamber has not granted leave for this cross-examination, so it seems fair to me to allow the Prosecution to have another ten minutes to ask a few question and at five to 3.00 I will give the Defence the floor to proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I actually ask the clock actually starts ticking when I ask my first question. By the time the witness gets in here and we get started, we might be close to ten to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Re, I can see the clock. It's right in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you can hear the interpretation. Looking at the clock, you've got until two minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, yesterday I was asking you some questions about what happened in Dusina and some questions about -- and you marked on a diagram where Zvonko Rajic's body was found. What I want to ask you is what happened after Zvonko Rajic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. The witness never said that Zvonko Rajic had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened after it was apparent that Zvonko Rajic, who had previously been shot in the legs by you, was lying dead on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I was withdrawn from the field with my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Geler?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was Geler?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public prosecutor from Travnik had more information about that, on the occasion when I gave a statement to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. That was on the 18th of December, 2000; you gave an affidavit to the public prosecutor in Travnik about the events in Dusina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you sign add copy of the affidavit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed a copy, although I never read the entire document until the time when you provided it to me here. That's the first time I saw the entire copy of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness BA, I was just asking you who was Geler. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about who Geler is or was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Geler in Dusina on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He was a soldier from what brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was in the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you see him in Dusina on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road up there. I don't remember exactly which part. The road leading to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just tell us -- the road was leading to where, please. Just repeat that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which part of the road I saw him on. I don't exactly remember the exact stretch of the road, so I wouldn't want to say where it was leading to. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember being told something about Geler doing something on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anything was said about him having done something on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you don't remember, are you saying that you don't remember now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't remember what was told to me on that day when I met him, when we were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you have recorded what someone told you about what Geler had done in another document, would looking at that document assist to refresh your memory as to what you were told about Geler?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the third question I've heard, and it's a leading question. I'm only reacting now, though, because the Prosecutor is yet again attempting to show the witness documents from a previous case. And as we were told by the Prosecution yesterday, he has spoken to the witness over a period of two days and provided him with copies of the statements for him to review. We have now been told by the witness that in a conversation before the trial the Prosecution provided him with those statements. And I don't think that there is any reason for providing the witness with documents to refresh his memory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's ruling at page 89 on Wednesday last week was that "to the extent to which the examination-in-chief is oral, the previous statement should not be presented to the witness during that stage and be used to possibly correct his answers. Therefore, it is not possible to produce that type of document during the examination-in-chief." And my learned colleague, Mr. Withopf, asked Your Honour the Presiding Judge for clarification of the decision and asked Your Honours to define the ambit of the ruling. This is at page 533 -- I said a moment 89. I should have said 532. Your Honours' definitive ruling is at page 533 of the transcript, where Your Honour the Presiding Judge ruled: "No, it only applies --" I'm sorry. I'll just go back to the question. The question of Mr. Withopf was: "Just for clarification, does this decision apply for prior statements only or does it apply for different documents?" And Your Honour the Presiding Judge's ruling was: "No, it only applies to prior statements collected within the framework of an investigation conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor. Other documents obviously may be produced during the examination." Now, that's the -- that's the Trial Chamber's ruling. I'm not attempting to ask the witness about any documents produced by the Office of the Prosecutor in -- within the framework of an investigation conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor. That's in respect of that part of Mrs. Residovic's objection. The second part is -- or the first objection was as to leading. There is no other way of getting a witness to that point in relation to another document unless you lead the witness to the fact that they have made a statement and asked them about their memory. That is the only way you could make -- you could actually get them to that point. So it has to be leading. It's one of those exceptional areas where any party may lead a witness to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this issue is concerned, with regard to the documents which are part of the list that was provided to the Defence before the trial, naturally the Defence, which had the opportunity of becoming familiar with this documents and had no comments to make, in such cases the documents can be produced. But the documents that the Defence has never seen can't be used by you. You can't present them unless you have informed the Defence in advance that you have the intention of presenting these documents. If necessary, if the need arises, it's up to the Defence to raise objections. But when a witness is being heard to present documents to the witness, documents which the Defence has never seen, this raises a problem if the Defence is not aware of the contents of these documents. This is what was said. As far as leading questions are concerned, as you know you must pose questions which are not leading or which don't suggest an answer that would correspond to the question. It must be up to the witness to judge the question and to answer the question freely. So there is an art to phrasing questions which consist of, obviously, not posing leading questions. So without asking a leading question, one can obtain a result by posing a series of questions which will elicit an answer from a witness. But if the question suggests an answer, then the Defence has the right to object. And if the Defence proceeds in the same manner, obviously the Prosecution will also object. So this concerns the way of questioning a witness. You have to avoid suggesting answers. The witness must answer the questions freely. Very well. As the objections took three minutes, I grant you another three minutes, and we will conclude at three minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Defence is fully aware of the contents of the documents I'm referring to. They've been provided with them a long time ago, and are fully on notice that they may form part of the testimony of this witness at the appropriate point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was, Witness BA, about your recording your recollection in relation to what happened in Dusina. Now, I'm asking you whether you recorded your recollections of what happened in Dusina anywhere, apart from in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A statement was given to the public prosecutor in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us you no longer had any memory of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've just lost the question, Your Honour. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- of being told what Geler -- of anything that Geler may have done on the day. I wish to show you a copy of a statement which you provided to the Travnik prosecutor, an affidavit, a signed affidavit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, we are in a situation which is very particular. I think that it requires the Defence to comment on the situation at this stage. And I would prefer if the witness left the courtroom for us to address this issue yet again, because it is only having an adverse effect on the testimony that we're hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you will leave a minute and you will come back a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, with regard to the witness who is with us today and who has been with us for three days now, I'd like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the Prosecution has had contact with the accused before he came to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Prosecution or the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, with the witness, Mr. President. But in the course of this preparation for the testimony, which as my colleague said was spread over a couple of days, they obtained from the witness certain notes on the testimony and they were already aware of the fact that the witness was going to make certain statements and they knew that they wouldn't be the same as what was contained in the statements that they possessed. So this new testimony of the witness -- this new statement, because these were notes that the Defence should have been provided with -- the Defence was never provided with this new statement. That's the first thing I want to say. And the second thing I want to raise is that the Prosecution is examining the witness and the Prosecution is well aware of the fact that the members of the Trial Chamber have the statement which they were able to see before the witness appeared in the courtroom. The Prosecution asks the witness a certain number of questions, and from the out-start, at the very beginning, when the very first questions were being put to the witness, the Prosecution was in a position to see that the witness was not providing them with the responses that they wanted or with the answers that one could have seen in documents that the Prosecution and Defence possess. And the Judges have had the opportunity of seeing these documents. So this situation requires three comments on the part of the Defence, apart from the fact that the Prosecution has concluded its examination, but you decided to be fair and grant them more time to proceed with more questions. The three comments are as follows: The first one, which is not as important as the others, concerns the resources of the Tribunal. From the very beginning of this trial, a number of arguments have been raised by the Prosecution concerning the fact that it was necessary to save the Tribunal's resources, that it was not necessary to waste time, and that it was necessary to do everything to improve the procedure. So we proceeded to examine a witness for a period of two day although we knew very well that this witness was not providing the questions that the Prosecution wanted to hear -- was not providing the answers that the Prosecution wanted to hear. It has taken two days and now we are being asked to say that the witness is an adverse witness; I think that's the term they used. This is not the most important matter -- a hostile witness. This is not the most important matter. The important matter is that you have a witness who came before you in good faith. The witness was well informed, both by the Prosecution and by the Chamber, both by the Prosecution and by the Chamber, that it was his duty to tell the truth and that what was important was his testimony here before the Trial Chamber. The witness was informed of this on a number of occasions. We think, Mr. President, that the procedure followed by the Prosecution amounts to undermining to a certain extent this witness's testimony. If they want to claim that this witness is a hostile witness, they could have done this at an earlier stage, but they examined the witness for two days and this places the witness in a very difficult situation since he has testified for two days. And now, instead of stopping him when the first opportunity arose, instead of telling him, "Witness, stop, we want to show you a document," instead of doing this immediately, they wanted for two days to raise this matter. And this is why I want to say that you can't play with witnesses like this, witnesses who have been through quite terrifying experiences in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and witnesses who have come to testify before this Chamber. We have discussed this possibility. The Prosecution asked you to declare that the witness was a hostile one. Following this request, you said that we were now in a position to cross-examine the witness before allowing the Prosecution to re-examine, which would be the normal procedure and then afterwards to submit a written motion with regard to declaring that the witness was a hostile one. For our part, we have asked for this procedure to be confirmed and we salute it because we believe that the cross-examination that we are preparing to conduct will make it possible to demonstrate the high possibility that what he has stated before this Trial Chamber reflects the truth, more than the statements that he may have made before an investigator from the Tribunal. And this cross-examination -- well, we informed you yesterday that it wouldn't take very long. But we believe that it will be sufficient to allow you to come to the conclusion that perhaps this witness -- that the fact that his answers do not correspond to those that he may have given on some other occasion -- this does not necessarily mean that the witness is not telling the truth. And today, with regard to -- he has mentioned a new statement given to the public prosecutor in Travnik. We believe, Mr. President, that this statement is concerned by a new oral decision of last week, which -- according to which we said that we would not use a statement to refresh the witness's memory. We could discuss the meaning of terms for a long time in order to determine whether your decision covers all statements and that is the Prosecution's intention, given that they are now submitting a request to have this decision -- the Trial Chamber's reconsidered. So I do not think that it is really the right time and place to try and discuss about the meaning of the terms -- of the words of one of the Trial Chamber's decisions. With regard to important legal issues, it is necessary to have this in written form, and we are preparing to do this, because we have been informed that a motion has been filed by the Prosecution and we will respond to it as rapidly as possible, as my colleague has said. The fact that we don't have the statement from the -- given to the prosecutor in Travnik doesn't change anything. The decisions that have been taken before this Trial Chamber means that the Prosecution has obtained certain concessions. We are glad that the Chamber has granted the Prosecution another ten minutes to go back to the subject and to try to undermine the testimony of a witness who is before you. Our cross-examination will allow you to see that perhaps the witness has not lied, which is what the Prosecution is attempting to say before this Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is a complete misunderstanding as to what the Prosecution was attempting to do. My learned friend Mr. Bourgon has spoken for about ten minutes on something we weren't doing. Your Honours's ruling is quite clear. As I said, Mr. Withopf specifically asked Your Honours what it applied to, and Your Honours said we sought that specific clarification, statements collected within the framework of an investigation collected by the OTP. The statement to which I wish to refer the witness is not a statement made within the frameworks of the OTP. It is an affidavit provided to the court in Travnik -- please let me finish, Mr. Bourgon -- in the course of an investigation in Zenica during the sorts of trials Mrs. Residovic referred to yesterday or the day before in relation to the protective-measures application. The Defence are aware of these trials and the investigations going on in Zenica and Travnik. In relation to -- Mr. Bourgon, please let me finish. In relation to whether or not the Defence have the statement, the Defence has the statement. It has been provided to them twice. We have the receipts. My case manager is looking for the receipt now which the two Defence or one of them signed for receiving a copy of it; firstly, on the 14th of October this year and secondly, again, on the 4th of December. In the context -- the second time was in the context of this witness's proposed evidence. The Defence are not being taken by surprise in any way. This witness has given several statements. This second statement is not covered by the earlier ruling of the Trial Chamber. And we had a very specific ruling on that. Mr. Bourgon also made a comment which is just completely inaccurate, and that is -- he said, "The Prosecution was already aware, after having a conference that the witness was going to make certain statements and they knew that they wouldn't be the same as what was contained in the statements that they possessed." I have no idea how Mr. Bourgon could possibly know what was going on in my head when I introduced the witness and started asking him questions and discovered that some of them were a little bit -- the answers were different to the answers he'd given me two hours before. I didn't know that, and I don't know how Mr. Bourgon could anticipate that I could have known that. I am not attempting to go behind Your Honours' ruling of last -- the Trial Chamber's ruling of last week. I'm attempting to refresh the witness's memory from another document, which is not covered by Your Honours' ruling in relation to showing a witness out out-of-court statements. It's a completely different issue. Mr. Bourgon also addressed Your Honour as if I was trying to undermine or have the witness declared hostile, despite Your Honours' ruling last night. Nothing is further from the truth. I am simply asking the witness, having established that the witness no longer has any recollection of what happened in relation to Geler or what was said about Geler, and that he has in fact recorded what happened in Dusina in another document, whether looking at that document would refresh his memory. I'm not attempting to undermine the witness in any way. I'm attempting to do what is normal -- what is the established practice before the International Tribunal: If a witness has forgotten something and the recollection has been recorded somewhere else, first you ascertain whether he has no memory; then, secondly, whether it has been recorded somewhere; then whether looking at it would, in fact, revive his memory; then you show him the document. That's all I was attempting to do. That's a normal procedure. And as far as the Prosecution can ascertain - and it's in today's filing - we've surveyed civil and common-law jurisdiction, international ones, the East Timor Tribunal and this jurisdiction -- in fact, this Tribunal, and it's permitted everywhere. Your Honours have made a specific ruling about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- about prior to OTP statements. We are sticking to that ruling and we are staking to Your Honours' ruling last night. We are attempting to do something completely different. And it relates to the leave I sought from Your Honour in relation to Dusina and what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If I may briefly. And this might be of some assistance. The Defence position is quite simply that this statement, like any other statement, should not be put to the witness now to allow him to refresh his memory. And that's, we submit, entirely in accordance with Your Honours' previous ruling, which was clarified to the extent, as Mr. Re has referred, that we are dealing here with prior statements collected - I think "collected" is the important word - within the framework of an investigation conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor. So all statements that are collected within that investigation should not be allowed to be put to the witness once he's in the witness box. And that would include, in our submission, the statement which was collected by the Prosecution during its investigation. It's appended to the statement of the witness, and it concerns exactly the same events as are in his statement. And our simple submission is that Your Honour has ruled no documents which are statements which allow the witness to refresh his memory should be put to him during examination-in-chief. The purpose of staying, as Your Honour did, that other documents may obviously be produced in examination, in our submission, would mean that exhibits, maps, documents that might come from the archives, your ruling obviously was not there to prevent those kinds of documents being put to a witness which the witness could introduce. And that is the interpretation which we think is clear and simple which should be put on your -- Your Honours' ruling. Of course, this matter might be litigated again in the future. But as things stand, that is the ruling, and in our submission the statement cannot now be put to the witness. Your Honour, finally, just on the point of hostile witnesses, I agree that this has nothing to do with hostile witnesses now, this particular argument. However, I think it is significant that the Prosecution have indicated to Your Honours that they wish to regard this witness as a hostile witness, and that can only mean that they no longer wish to rely on this witness as a witness of truth. Put bluntly, if they were able to cross-examine him, they would say that he is now lying. And they can't have it both ways. They can't say he's a liar and then also start asking him questions about a -- a previous statement, seeking to then rely on his evidence to prove their case. It's one or the other. And at the moment they're somewhere in between, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just correct something my learned friend Mr. -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should wholly like to join in what Mr. Dixon said. We agree; we consider all statements that a person who appears as a witness before this Tribunal, which were given to state organs, whether they be in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Tribunal, are witness statements. They are not documents. And as this is an important question and the Prosecution has also filed a motion, I think that a different interpretation should not be accepted until we hear a final ruling from you, Your Honours, or perhaps from the Appeals Chamber. Secondly, the Prosecutor, in response to the words uttered by my colleague that the Prosecution prior to the witness's entering knew that the witness would not be answering these questions asked how we knew that. And the Prosecutor last night, in explaining the reasons for which he is -- for which he wants to declare the witness a hostile witness - on page 17 of the unofficial transcript - said that the witness at the beginning would just make short changes to the statement, ones of translation and things of that kind, but that by noon he began changing the version he gave to the Prosecution. So my colleague, Mr. Bourgon, in explaining the knowledge gained by the Prosecution started by quoting the words uttered by the Prosecution before this Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing that happened between my saying farewell to the witness, "see you in court", and him arriving in court a conference with Defence counsel, Mrs. Residovic. Up until that moment I had no idea when he came into the box that his evidence would be any different to what he told me at noon when I said goodbye to him. I just want to correct something Mr. Dixon said. It doesn't necessarily follow if a witness is declared hostile that the Prosecution would accuse the witness of lying. And in fact it's of very little forensic purpose for the Prosecutor to suggest to the witness he is lying. The purpose of a declaration of adversity or hostility such as to allow the Prosecution to examine, as opposed to examine -- ask non-leading questions in examination-in-chief, is to elicit a reason for any differences between a prior statement and a -- an in-court statement and to try to assist the Trial Chamber in getting to the truth of the matter. I can assure the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has no present intention, and as long as I'm conducting the examination of Witness BA, to suggest that he's lying. Nothing will be gained if the Prosecution were to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this debate concerning the Defence and the Prosecution, it could go on for days, because if one declaration leads to a response by the opposite side, and that goes on and on, I'll have to limit you taking the floor. But I will give you the floor one more time and then the Chamber will state its views.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was quoting the words of the Prosecutor on page 38. And with your permission, at 2.15 Mr. Ibrisimovic and myself saw the witness for ten minutes. I hope that the Prosecutor knew what he was saying when he said what he just said. I have no further comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber -- I would like to note the following situation: This witness has, within the framework of a motion, said outside the solemn declaration, said to a representative of the OTP -- or rather, made statements to him which were mentioned in certain paragraphs. And it is upon this document that the Prosecution wanted to conduct an examination-in-chief so that the witness could roughly state the weight of that document. The Chamber, Trial Chamber, took note of the fact from the very beginning that the witness said very few things and even refused to answer certain very ordinary questions. However, the witness seems to have taken up that position, a position taken under the solemn declaration, under oath. The witness was cautioned and said that he could be held up for false testimony, for perjury, and contempt of court. He was cautioned of his rights and he said that protective measures had been accorded to him so that nothing he said in the courtroom would be heard outside and this -- that he didn't run any risks. He was also told that if he stated certain things they couldn't be used in evidence against him before this Tribunal, and we also added before national courts either. So the witness was completely and comprehensibly informed of the different facets of the problem. He was informed by the Prosecution of why he was here, to confirm what he had stated earlier on. The Defence saw him for a period of ten minutes. As we weren't there, we don't know what was said. But he did see the Defence for a short period of time. And he was under the solemn declaration and under oath, and it was under oath that he made his testimony and answered questions from the Prosecution. However, the Prosecution went as far as to qualify him as a hostile witness at one point. Three days later, at a certain point, the Prosecution wanted to rely on a document that the Trial Chamber discovered which came from the Travnik court, and we heard your views. Both parties expressed their views with respect to this document. It was produced -- the exhibit was produced before the proceedings. I'm trying to find the said document. The Prosecution tells us today that that testimony was recorded under oath. It would be simpler for the Prosecution at the beginning of the examination-in-chief to refresh the witness's memory by asking him questions and asking him the following: Before coming to The Hague, did you -- were you the object of an investigation? And give us a yes or no answer. That would have been the question. Were you taken before a magistrate; yes or no? Now, if he said yes, he was taken before a magistrate, then the next question would have been: Did you testify under oath? And then we could have had a yes or no answer. Could you tell the Court what you said to the magistrate. So that is how the affair could perhaps have been conducted, and we could have learnt on that basis. Now, as we are having a pleading - we weren't there, so we can't say - but the Defence is contesting the production of a document of this nature, which of course hampers the Defence in its cross-examination. But as I explained to you yesterday, it would be possible if the Trial Chamber so decides to allow the witness to come back, with other foundations laid. And I should like to remind you that with respect to Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure, supplementary evidence, it too can decide to recall the witness. Therefore, if we find that a witness is doing this, I don't think we need exert pressure on the witness. And yesterday on several occasions we saw that the witness did restrict his answers and did not wish to elaborate further. Therefore, if the Trial Chamber considers it necessary to recall the witness, to have him come back to The Hague, we shall do so. So we shall now put an end to this debate, because we need a trial ruling on several motions. It is now 3.30, and I think we ought to start the cross-examination of this witness without further adieu. So I should like to ask the usher to bring the witness into court. And I think the witness said they would be taking half an hour. If they do so, they can take a break at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're now going to be answering questions put to you by the Defence, and it is the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic who's going to start off by asking you questions and then you will hear from Mr. Kubura's Defence team. Later on the Prosecution has the right to redirect. The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. BA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I saw you for the first time the day before yesterday for ten minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was even ten minutes. It was barely ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, you and I speak the same language. We understand each other. And you can answer my questions quickly. But I should like to ask you to make pauses between my question and your answer, to wait for the interpretation to finish because otherwise it will be very difficult for the interpreters to interpret and for the other people in the courtroom to follow the proceedings. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask, in order to facilitate conversation, our communication, I should like to ask you to look at a map which shows the Zenica area. The Defence has a sufficient number of copies for Their Honours and for the Prosecution. So could you place the map in front of you and on the ELMO as well so that we can see it on our screens. Mr. BA, would you mark with a pencil the location of Zenica, and put number "1" if you can; if you're able to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, you lived in the Zenica municipality, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were other ethnic groups living in Zenica too: The Serbs, the Croats, the Bosniaks, Jews; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zenica and Sarajevo, as the capital of the republic, was linked by an asphalt road, and we called it the motorway, and it passed through Kakanj and Visoko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please place an arrow on the map to mark that road and place the number "2" beside the arrow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, the Army of Republika Srpska temporarily occupied the road from Visoko running to Sarajevo, and you couldn't go to Sarajevo from Zenica taking that road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could reach Sarajevo by another road, the road running from the confluence of the Lasva River, which was called the Lasva-network road through Busovaca and Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once the road via Busovaca was blocked, you could reach the area around Sarajevo only by taking a mountain road via Lasva and Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the Lasva junction were to be blocked, you couldn't go to Sarajevo from Zenica at all, could you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right. I don't think you could, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, from Zenica to Travnik - and Travnik is second-largest town in the region - the main road led across the Lasva junction down the Lasva River Valley through Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified before this Trial Chamber for two days, and during your testimony here in court you said that it was the task of your unit to provide security at the Lasva junction because it was such an important junction; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, from Zenica to Travnik you could take a mountain asphalt road, which went via Ovnak, Guca Gora, and the surrounding hamlets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct, Mr. BA, that in January 1993 the HVO -- or rather, the Croatian Defence Council, blocked the road running towards Busovaca and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO held checkpoints at Ovnak as well and so was able to block the links from Zenica to Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: By blocking the roads running towards Busovaca and the road across Ovnak, Travnik and Zenica were completely cut off; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go back a little bit, Mr. BA, to discuss the conflicts that arose between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. Do you know that in the second half of January 1993 armed conflicts began between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in the area of Busovaca and Kiseljak? Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not personally aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, you said before this Tribunal that the commander of your unit was Elvedin Camdzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you knew that in December 1992 in a battle at Visegrad, together -- taking part together with you, that there were some Mujahedin, foreigners taking part; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, you don't personally know where the Mujahedin came from, nor under whose control they were placed in December 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that I kept trying to explain to the Prosecutor, but I'm afraid I wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what you want to say is that you don't know under whose control and command they actually were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you did know that in December 1992 the Mujahedin had arrested certain officers from the 7th Muslim Brigade and officers of the BH army from Visoko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, you also said that on the 25th of January, 1993, in the evening hours, following orders from -- you left Lasva in the direction of Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that was the exact date, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it was the day before the armed conflict broke out between your unit and the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you took a byroad going behind the hill to reach the village of Lasva, is that right, a roundabout road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't go to the village of Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant the village of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had received orders to take this bypass and not to move through inhabited areas, Donja Visnjica and Brdo, for example, because you didn't want an armed conflict to break out with the HVO or with the local population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your orders were to reach the separation line without having to enter into any fighting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that on the 25th of January in Dusina two members of the BH army had been captured but at the time you didn't know their names; is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew that a member of your own unit had been captured; that is to say, from the 7th Muslim Brigade by the name of Zijad -- Camdzic [phoen]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned his name. I knew that there was one member, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The armed conflict with members of the HVO began after the members of the HVO had killed your commander, Elvedin Camdzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the HVO, after that, killed another fighter, who tried to come to Camdzic's assistance. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Asked by my learned colleague of the Prosecution, you said that at Brdo there were about ten members of your own unit there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among those fellow combatants was Abdullah Colakovic, Emir, nicknamed Mire, and five or six other soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the individuals whose names I mentioned knew that you were engaged in another assignment and that you weren't a witness as to how Zvonko Rajic died; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although in your own unit there was a man called Dizdarevic, nicknamed Camara, because he had other obligations that particular day he wasn't in the area of Dusina that particular day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, I'm going to move on and ask you something else now. You know that during that period of time in the area of Zenica there was a large number of refugees and the population almost doubled? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that there was a lot of theft, that private property was being stolen, and that this was happening in large numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your command, both of the battalion and of the brigade, on several occasions issued orders prohibiting theft and other unlawful acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions you were warned -- you were cautioned about the necessity to adhere to the Geneva Conventions. That's what you stated. Is that right -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. BA, you are aware of the fact that in 1993, especially in the first half of that year, there was much abuse with regard to wearing the insignia of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said about the badges, the insignia. I said that you could obtain them on the road. They were on sale.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are probably aware of the fact that some people before courts in Zenica were prosecuted for having pretended to be members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Do you know anything more about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about certain persons. I have information about certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, would it be correct to say that you didn't know General Enver Hadzihasanovic and that you've seen him here in this courtroom for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. BA, when my colleague Ibrisimovic and I spoke to you, did we ask you to only speak the truth before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's ten to 4.00. It might be best to have a break right now. And we shall recommence at 4.20 and Mr. Kubura's Defence shall take the floor then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence. You may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we'll only have a few questions for the Witness BA. Since there's a document that might reveal this witness's identity, could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go into private session. Madam Registrar, could with go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look -- Witness BA, His Honour Judge Antonetti just asked you a question about a distinction between remembering and not knowing. Your response was: "A. Your Honour, I'm only proving interpretation of what was recorded in previous statements. I'm only correcting things that weren't properly recorded. On several occasions, I tried to draw the attention to certain parts of the statement in this case to the Prosecutor, but the Prosecutor just ignored these items and spoke about what he was interested in." Now, Witness BA, I want to show you a document that you marked during a conference between the -- sorry, after the conference we had on Sunday. It's your statement which I gave you to take back to your hotel and to mark on it anything you wanted corrected. Can I just show you the statement with your markings on it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop there, please. Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you've just raised the question of re-examination, which is in accordance with the Rules of this Tribunal. Cross-examination [as interpreted] can -- must be restricted to questions posed by the Defence in the course of its cross-examination. With regard to this question and showing the statement, this is not a matter I addressed in the course of my cross-examination. As far as we know, Mr. Kubura's Defence didn't do so either. Therefore, I'm asking the Trial Chamber not to allow the Prosecution to put such a question because it doesn't arise from the Defence's cross-examination. This brings us back to the subject that we discussed a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it -- Your Honours, with great respect, Your Honour the Presiding Judge asked a question. Re-examination occurrence after -- Your Honours, of course, can ask questions at any time. The normal practice before this Tribunal is if the Bench asks questions, either party is given an opportunity to clarify anything which is in the interest of that party with the witness, because as Your Honour the Presiding Judge, correctly remarked last week, it's more of an adversarial proceeding here than an inquisitorial one. Re-examination, in one sense, relates, of course, to the questions in cross-examination posed by the Defence. And I have several questions I would ask the witness. However, I'm asking the witness to clarify something as a result of a question Your Honour asked the witness and something Your Honour would not have known of when Your Honour posed the question to the witness, to clarify the issue which the witness raised about the Prosecution not correcting certain matters which the witness raised with the Prosecution. This is a -- an inquiry, a quest for the truth. And the document I wish to show the witness, only for the purposes of his telling -- informing Your Honours what he marked on it -- that is, the fact that he marked certain portions of the document -- I don't want to go into it. It's only to clarify the question Your Honour asked, which either party of course is entitled to do. And I wouldn't object to my learned colleague Mrs. Residovic standing up and asking a further question, with leave, as a result of Your Honour's question. The Prosecution states on the record it certainly doesn't object to the Defence seeking leave to request further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as this matter is concerned, the Defence is claiming that in the course of the cross-examination the Prosecution can ask questions again but the Defence says that these questions must regard questions that arose in the course of the cross-examination. According to Rule 85, it says that after the examination-in-chief the witness can be cross-examined and re-examined. So it's not an additional examination, it's additional examination [as interpreted] in the French version. So I come to the conclusion that the Prosecution may pose other questions, questions other than those that were addressed by the Defence. But having said that, there is another problem that arises and that is that the Prosecution wants to show the witness, in order "to refresh the witness's memory" - in invented commas - to Prosecution wants to show the witness a document that the witness signed no later than last weekend. This document concerns a statement taken by the OTP several months ago. The last time, we decided that as the procedure was oral, it couldn't be presented at any stage -- that the witness's written statement couldn't be presented to the witness at any stage. So I don't see any reason to modify our position. Moreover, within the framework of discussions between the witness and the Prosecution or the witness and the Defence, there are rules concerning confidentiality and normally one party, especially when testifying, must inform the other party if the need arises of the necessity of producing the said document. They must be informed in advance. I have no proof that this was done and that the witness has agreed to the matter, because the witness can always argue that his confidence has been betrayed in the course of an interview which was confidential and the right to this confidentiality is guaranteed. So I won't grant leave for this document to be shown to the witness, but you can ask questions concerning the document in order to refresh the witness's memory. But we should add, as the witness said, his memory is very good; I do not see why it would be necessary to refresh the witness's memory, since he told us a while ago that he made a distinction between main issues and secondary issues. And his encounter with the OTP is certainly an important event for him, so he must remember it. Nevertheless, the Prosecution has leave to ask this witness questions. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. The Prosecution's issue is with the witness saying "just ignored." That's the point of my questions. I make it quite clear I'm not attempting to refresh the witness's memory in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness BA, there's no dispute, I hope, in terms of my leading, that we had a conference on Sunday and Monday before you gave your evidence, during which you looked at a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Bourgon objecting to leading? I -- I'm trying to get to the point very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You should have asked him whether you met a few days ago. The answer would have been yes. Or, "Did I show you a document; yes or no?" But your question, in fact, is suggesting an answer. I think that's what you were going to say. Very well. You can sit down. We have saved some time. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness BA, did the Prosecution -- did you confer with the Prosecution before you gave your evidence here over the last -- within the last few days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it -- can you tell the Court what day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sunday, Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember how long we conferred for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first meeting was short, and the second one lasted for three or four hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer. The interpreter didn't hear you quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I see it's necessary for me to intervene again. The questions asked by my colleague are leading questions, the objective of which is precise; either to make a distinction between what was said when they conferred with the witness confidentially and what the witness said in front of this Trial Chamber. If the Prosecution wants to use such a procedure, this amounts to cross-examination. For the Trial Chamber to allow him to do this I think the witness should leave again so the Prosecution can explain what the objective of these questions are, so that they can show why they're asking such questions. If they are trying to establish that the witness did not say -- tell the truth, that is the objective of cross-examination, and this is not permitted in the course of re-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what the Defence has said is pertinent, and the only questions that -- the only questions that are allowed are for the witness to confirm that you met. You can address certain issues. But it shouldn't go beyond that scope. But I think the witness is quite prepared to say that you did confer with each other. The conversations you had with the witness may have been private and he might think that private conversations should not be discussed in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know where Mr. Bourgon gets the idea that I was attempting to cross-examine the witness. I was asking the witness the questions Your Honour asked me or permitted me to ask in accordance with Your Honour's directions as to whether or not I showed him a document and whether he made any markings on it. That is it, period. The second point is in relation to the confidentiality or otherwise of conversations with the witness. There are no confidential conversations between a witness who is to give evidence before this Trial Chamber as to the extent and scope of his evidence. The only thing which could possibly be confidential may be things relating to his identity. Everything that is said between the Prosecution, its investigators, and a potential witness is disclosable under Rule 68 and Rule 66(A). The contents of the proofing session are also matters which we should and must disclose to the Defence if there is anything which deviates from the information we have provided the Defence in advance that we intend to call from a witness. We did not provide the Defence with anything which indicated there was to be a deviation because there was to be no deviation. There were several minor corrections on matters which I wasn't even going to lead. In relation to the witness I called last week, after having a conference with the witness, we provided the Defence with a proofing note of an additional matter which had arisen during our conference. So can I make it quite clear - the Prosecution makes it quite clear to the Trial Chamber and to my learned friends from the Defence - there are no confidential discussions between witnesses and the Prosecution as to the content of their evidence. Prosecutors have a duty to disclose the content of their conversations with witnesses; that's why we take notes. That's why we disclose them.
